sourceText: cells: Nt, Tc On night 8, the course began with a prohibition: no one was allowed to solve the problem before they could describe who would pay for the solution. Only then did Aster open the FORWARD-CHEELA sector. Orin is accelerated on a neutron star and lives for centuries during an interval in which his siblings do not finish a sentence. The memorial bore the name of Robert L. Forward — Dragon's Egg precisely to keep the genealogy of the idea visible. Aster considered it indecent for a late civilization to treat the imagination of the past as anonymous ore: authors did not own the futures, but they deserved to remain on the map as points of intellectual origin. Aster had forbidden gratuitous scenery. Every exotic property had to leave traces in metabolism, infrastructure, and institutions; otherwise it was merely a special effect. Kesh built his classifications as instruments of falsification: a good category had to state what it did not cover, not merely what it could absorb. Tala was the first inhabitant to contradict them. Tala had neither access to their archives nor any interest in hyperdimensional pedagogy; there was a local problem, with deadlines, relatives, and consequences. For Tala, the speculative mechanism was not an ‘idea.’ 67 It was the environment in which one had to decide what one was willing to risk losing. The problem closed quickly around them: When he returns, the people he loved are history to everyone else, and temporal scale has become a form of moral inequality. There was no clean option. Every intervention shifted the cost between persons, eras, or definitions of personhood; and refusing to intervene was itself a choice made by those who could leave. Kesh opened the analytical layer of the Table for a few seconds. The active cells were Nt — Neutron Life: organisms live in degenerate matter; Tc — Cognitive Time: different minds live at radically different speeds. Course references included Robert L. Forward — Dragon's Egg; Robert L. Forward; uploads. The rule was strict: naming a work did not substitute for an explanation. They had to identify the mechanism that could migrate into another story and the consequences that could not be copied without remainder. Vela broke the first consensus. ‘If we can save the situation only by making the world resemble us more closely, we have not demonstrated the superiority of our solution. We have demonstrated only our power.’ Tern answered without raising their voice: ‘Sometimes the ethical question is whether we are entitled to know enough to optimize.’ It was not a pedagogical quarrel. Over the last nights, the children’s differences had become incompatible political programs. Aster felt the Hunger precisely when an explanation closed too elegantly. A perfect theory reduced surprise, and surprise was the last symptom that something before her had not yet become part of her. 68 THE PERIODIC TABLE OF SPECULATIVE IDEAS The children had noticed that their disagreement calmed her more than any extravagant universe did. Vela evaluated the solution not by efficiency but by the differences it made invisible. She found one: a local minority for whom the proposed “improvement” destroyed a practice with no equivalent. Optimizing the average concealed a small and perfectly legal extinction. The night did not end in victory. Orin refuses ever again to accept processing speed as an excuse for inattention toward slow civilizations. Aster recorded the decision in the world’s provenance register and, more importantly, allowed its inhabitants to contest it. For several eras she had been learning something that seems banal to lesser powers: technical reversibility is not the same as biographical reversibility. Tern remained a few seconds after the others. A very faint deviation repeated in the sector’s background noise, too coherent to be thermal and too useless to be a teaching signal. He did not tell Aster. It was the first thing he possessed solely by not sharing it. For the course, Kesh also linked the night to the COUPLING operator. In the Table, periodicity did not mean that the same objects reappeared, but that the same operation — makes previously independent domains determine one another — could recur across different families. Thus a copy of a body, a copy of a mind, a copy of a world, and a copy of a history were not the same phenomenon, but they shared a conceptual chemistry. 69 Vela introduced the propagation test: if you remove the speculative idea and nothing in the institutions, relationships, or vocabulary has to be rewritten, the idea has remained scenery. Kesh introduced the opposite test: if the idea seems to explain every detail, you have overcompressed the world. Between the two tests lay the region in which an element became fertile without becoming superstition. Marae added the refusal test. Who can say “no,” and what happens afterward? In universes with near-divine technology, that question often separated an instrument from a regime. A power that treats refusal as a data error can be benevolent in intention and totalitarian in structure. They left without an oral summary. Aster had abandoned the habit of closing every night with a thesis; some worlds were more honestly preserved as problems than as lessons. 70 THE PERIODIC TABLE OF SPECULATIVE IDEAS
